topic: Calvin H. Waller, Penn State class of 1905
fact: In June 1905, Calvin Hoffman Waller of Macon, Georgia, received an agriculture degree in Schwab Auditorium and became the first African American student known to have graduated from Penn State. He was 25. The university did not record students’ race, so the “first known” rests on the yearbook and what his classmates remembered. He had enrolled in 1899, after three Black agricultural schools, because the leading Southern programs were closed to him.
where: Darryl Daisey, who compiled the Penn State African American Chronicles, talked with The Daily Collegian about Waller in October 2024.
also: He also recorded Waller’s 1905 graduation in Penn State African American Firsts (August 2010).

topic: A letter from Penn State’s president about Calvin Waller
fact: In 1902, Penn State president George Atherton wrote Booker T. Washington that the college had “one young colored man” of such ability that Atherton had “no doubt that he will be prepared for a successful career.” That student was Calvin H. Waller. Accounts of Waller’s 1905 commencement give no sign that anyone marked the day as a first.
where: Darryl told The Daily Collegian about Atherton’s letter in an October 2024 interview on Waller.

topic: Mildred Settle Bunton, Penn State class of 1932
fact: When Mildred Settle Bunton transferred to Penn State in 1929, she was the only Black woman on campus. The seventh of nine children, she worked for faculty in exchange for room and board, stayed on the dean’s list, and in 1932 graduated with honors and the highest grades in home economics. She later earned a master’s in nutrition at Cornell.
where: Darryl spoke about her at the Penn State NAACP lecture “Penn State African American History… Shaping a Stronger Community Today,” on Feb. 23, 2017.

topic: The Bunton-Waller awards
fact: In September 1994 Penn State began the Mildred S. Bunton and Calvin Waller scholarship and fellowship programs, named for the first African American woman and the first African American man known to have graduated. The awards go to students who strengthen the university’s diversity.
where: Darryl compiled this entry in Penn State African American Firsts in August 2010, and he has lectured on both namesakes.
sourceLabel: Penn State African American Firsts, compiled by Darryl Daisey

topic: Cumberland “Cum” Posey Jr.
fact: Cumberland “Cum” Posey Jr. enrolled at Penn State in 1909 as the college’s first Black student athlete. He played freshman and varsity basketball and freshman baseball, then left after two years. He later owned the Homestead Grays and was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2006.
where: Darryl spoke about Posey at the Feb. 23, 2017 NAACP lecture and listed him in African American Firsts.

topic: Posey’s basketball dynasty before the Grays
fact: Before he built the Homestead Grays, Posey ran the Loendi Big Five basketball club. Loendi won the Colored Basketball World Championship four years in a row, from 1920 to 1923. Posey had already been the star, the booker, and the promoter.
where: The championship run is on the Penn State Black History timeline Darryl founded, and he discussed Posey in his 2017 campus lecture.

topic: The Frederick E. Douglass Association
fact: Students founded the Frederick E. Douglass Association in October 1967 to petition for an African American history course. Frederick B. Phillips was the first president. The next spring the university offered “The Negro and the American Experience,” a forerunner of Black Studies.
where: Darryl spoke about the Douglass Association at the Feb. 23, 2017 NAACP lecture and wrote the entry in African American Firsts.

topic: Twelve demands in Old Main, May 1968
fact: On May 13, 1968, about five weeks after Dr. King was assassinated, roughly 100 members of the Douglass Association brought 12 demands to the vice president for student affairs in Old Main: more Black students, Black faculty and coaches, and an African cultural studies program. The meeting lasted nearly three hours.
where: Darryl’s Penn State Black History timeline records the meeting, and he discussed the Douglass Association in his 2017 lecture.

topic: Lincoln Hall
fact: Lincoln Hall was an off-campus boarding house run by the Gifford family. In the 1940s it held about six to eight Black men at a time, sometimes half the Black students on campus. An unofficial rule kept Black men out of the residence halls until 1946. Roommates included Wally Triplett and Olympic sprinter Barney Ewell.
where: Darryl spoke about Lincoln Hall at the 2017 NAACP lecture and again on April 2, 2025. At the hall’s 2012 historical-marker ceremony he credited the Giffords with housing students the dorms would not take.

topic: Wally Triplett and Penn State football
fact: Wallace “Wally” Triplett became the first Black starter on the Penn State varsity football team on Nov. 17, 1945, and in 1946 the first Black player to earn a varsity letter in the sport there. He lived at Lincoln Hall when the dorms would not take him.
where: Darryl wrote those firsts in African American Firsts, and in 2020 he told Onward State about driving Triplett and his wife from the Lewistown station to the 2012 Black Alumni Reunion.

topic: The 1948 Cotton Bowl
fact: On Jan. 1, 1948, Triplett and teammate Dennie Hoggard became the first Black players in the Cotton Bowl, after Penn State refused to leave them home for the game in segregated Dallas. Triplett caught the tying touchdown in a 13–13 tie with SMU. The stadium chant “We Are… Penn State” came later: cheerleaders introduced it in 1976. The 1948 stand is a separate story.
where: Darryl has written and spoken about Triplett — in African American Firsts, in the Onward State interview, and in his 2011 All-Sports Museum talk on African American athletes and “lost legends.”
sourceLabel: Penn State, “Why we say We Are”

topic: The leather helmet Triplett would sign
fact: Triplett would not sign plastic helmets, because he had never played in one. Before the 2012 reunion, Darryl found two miniature leather helmets. Triplett signed both. Darryl kept one and gave the other to a scholarship auction. His 1949 collection also holds a signed photo and Triplett’s NFL rookie card.
where: Darryl told that story to Onward State for a June 17, 2020 feature on vintage Penn State memorabilia.

topic: Dave and Harry Alston
fact: In September 1941, brothers Dave and Harry Alston of Midland, Pennsylvania, joined the freshman football team, the first Black players to play football at Penn State. Dave was the star of that team. He died the next year from complications after a tonsillectomy, a few weeks before the varsity debut his coach had been talking up. Harry left school soon after.
where: Darryl spoke about the Alston brothers at “A History of Black Excellence at Penn State” on April 2, 2025, and he listed them in African American Firsts.

topic: Guion “Guy” Bluford
fact: On Aug. 30, 1983, Penn State aerospace graduate Guion S. “Guy” Bluford, class of 1964, rode Challenger’s STS-8 mission and became the first African American in space. It was also the shuttle program’s first night launch. He flew four missions and logged more than 688 hours in space. He has said Penn State also gave him an Air Force commission, a pilot’s license, and the meeting with his wife, Linda.
where: Darryl included Bluford in the April 2, 2025 lunch-and-learn at the HUB-Robeson Center.

topic: H. Jesse Arnelle, student body president
fact: In April 1954, basketball and football star H. Jesse Arnelle was elected all-university student body president by a wide margin. He was reported to be the first Black student to head the student government of a major predominantly white university.
where: Darryl spoke about Arnelle on April 2, 2025, and he wrote the election into African American Firsts.

topic: Jesse Arnelle’s scoring record, and a prize he turned down
fact: Arnelle’s 2,138 career points stood as Penn State’s basketball scoring record for 56 years, and he remains the school’s only basketball All-American of that era. He was the first Nittany Lion to play in the NBA. In 1968 he publicly turned down the first Alumni Association Award to protest weak minority recruitment. The next year he became the first Black member of the Board of Trustees, and in 1996 the first African American to chair it.
where: The record and the refused award are on the Black History timeline Darryl founded. He spoke about Arnelle at the April 2, 2025 program.

topic: Julie Cromitie
fact: On Feb. 26, 1964, Julie Cromitie was installed as the first Black president of the Association of Women Students, the body that coordinated cultural and educational life for Penn State’s women. In June 1965 she became the first Black student to receive the Ralph Dorn Hetzel Memorial Award, then the university’s highest student honor.
where: Darryl spoke about her at the April 2, 2025 history program and recorded both firsts in the 2010 list he compiled.

topic: Keegan-Michael Key
fact: Keegan-Michael Key earned a master of fine arts in theater from Penn State in 1996, after a bachelor of fine arts from the University of Detroit Mercy in 1993. He later co-created the sketch series Key & Peele.
where: Darryl spoke about Key at “A History of Black Excellence at Penn State” on April 2, 2025.

topic: The swim test that was never required
fact: For more than 48 years Penn State presented a swim test as if it were mandatory. On Feb. 11, 1982, Darryl, then a student in East Halls, questioned the policy and found it had never been a requirement at all. Dropping it removed what the Black History timeline calls a small barrier to minority recruitment.
where: He uncovered it, and The Daily Collegian quoted him that September: “I think it should be optional all the time.” The episode is an entry on the timeline he later built.

topic: April 4, 1968, in a first-grade classroom
fact: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. was shot in Memphis on April 4, 1968. In Oakland that afternoon, a crowd of about 50 young people gathered outside Toler Heights Elementary shouting “they shot him,” and bricks came through the first-grade windows. Darryl was almost seven. He later wrote that he began to learn who King was on the day he died.
where: Darryl wrote the account himself, in a forum essay for The Daily Collegian published April 10, 1985.

topic: The March on Washington, and a quiet house
fact: Darryl’s father, William Daisey, attended the 1963 March on Washington. His obituary says he sat about 25 feet from Dr. King. On the night of the assassination, Darryl wrote, the evening news left the Oakland house quiet, and his mother was the first to cry.
where: Darryl wrote the scene in his 1985 Collegian essay. The march is also in his father’s obituary, which the family-history talks draw on.

topic: Delaware’s 1875 Jim Crow law
fact: In 1875 Delaware legislators passed a Jim Crow law that made Black Delawareans second-class citizens, including in the schools. The legislature did not repeal it until 1963 — the same year Gloria Allen became the first Black graduate of Lewes High School.
where: On Feb. 22, 2025, Darryl laid out that timeline, from the 1875 law to Brown v. Board, while moderating a panel at Lewes Elementary. He also compiled it into the Lewes Delaware Black History Timeline.
sourceLabel: Lewes Delaware Black History Timeline, compiled by Darryl B. Daisey

topic: Twelve years between Brown and Lewes
fact: Brown v. Board of Education was decided in 1954. Lewes did not begin total desegregation of its public schools until September 1966, twelve years later. The first voluntary admissions of Black students to the formerly white-only schools came in September 1961.
where: Darryl moderated the Feb. 22, 2025 panel on that integration and wrote both dates into the city timeline he compiles.

topic: Nine children who opened the Lewes schools
fact: The students who integrated the Lewes public schools were six Allen children — Gloria, Wendy, Tony, Alfred, William, and James — and three Daisey children: William Jr., Sarah, and Deborah. Sarah started first grade and Deborah kindergarten. Reports from the time mention racist name-calling, and little violence. Gloria Allen graduated from Lewes High School in June 1963, the school’s first Black graduate.
where: Darryl moderated five of them, including his sisters Sarah and Deborah, on Feb. 22, 2025, and he wrote the names into the Lewes timeline.

topic: No Sussex County diploma until 1950
fact: Until 1950, no Sussex County school awarded a high school diploma to Black or Native American students. To finish, a student had to leave home for Howard High School in Wilmington or the high school department at Delaware State College. William Daisey boarded with his grandmother in Wilmington for his senior year at Howard.
where: Darryl presented the Daisey family history, including his father’s schooling, to the Lewes African American Heritage Commission on Feb. 16, 2023, and he recorded the 1950 change in the timeline he compiles.

topic: William C. Jason Comprehensive High School
fact: William C. Jason Comprehensive High School opened in Georgetown in 1950 for the Black and Native American students of Sussex County and served them through 1967. It began with grades 9 through 12 and added seventh and eighth grade in 1953.
where: Darryl compiled this into the Lewes Delaware Black History Timeline, updated June 2026.

topic: Johnnie Walker Beach
fact: During Delaware’s Jim Crow years, Lewes Beach 1 — now Savannah Beach — was reserved for white beachgoers, and Beach 2 for Black residents and visitors. In 1958 Johnnie Walker, a Georgia-born entrepreneur born in 1917, opened a restaurant and dance hall on Beach 2. It stayed open into the early 1970s. On Oct. 11, 2021, the mayor and council renamed the beach for him by a unanimous vote.
where: Darryl compiled the beach’s story into the Lewes timeline. As heritage-commission chair he spoke in August 2026 about delays to a pavilion planned for the site.
sourceLabel: City of Lewes, Johnnie Walker Beach

topic: The man who watched the beach
fact: Parents remembered Johnnie Walker watching Beach 2 so children could play, with lifeguards on duty and Walker himself nearby. He also ran a construction company and helped local families buy their first homes. He died on July 24, 1992. The old wooden pavilion, used for meals, dancing, worship, and baptisms, is the building the heritage commission wants rebuilt.
where: The city history page and the timeline Darryl compiles tell Walker’s story. Darryl has spoken about the pavilion as commission chair, including before the fifth Johnnie Walker Beach Day on Sept. 19, 2026.

topic: The Lewes Community Playground
fact: The Lewes Community Playground was dedicated on June 1, 1957, on land leased from Mayor Otis H. Smith, where Shipcarpenter Square now stands. The Jolly Jills, the Lewes Civic Club, and a junior-high parent group paid for equipment, a baseball diamond, and restrooms. Children played there until the land was sold in 1978. Black and white children were already playing baseball together on that field before the schools integrated.
where: Darryl emceed “This Used to Be My Playground” on Feb. 21, 2026, and he wrote the 1957 dedication into the city timeline.

topic: The Jolly Jills Memorial Day parade
fact: Beginning in May 1954, the Jolly Jills Social Club and Lewes Junior High sponsored a Memorial Day parade that ended at the open field where Shipcarpenter Square now stands. Bands and majorettes marched. Family photographs from the late 1950s show one of those parades.
where: Darryl has presented those photographs, including in his Feb. 16, 2023 family-history talk, and he compiled the parade into the Lewes timeline.

topic: Lewes’s Black Girl Scout troop
fact: In 1963 the Lewes Girl Scout troop still did not admit African American or Native American girls, so a group of mothers formed their own, with help from the existing troop. Shirley Daisey was one of the leaders. By the late 1960s the Lewes troops had desegregated and the separate troop disbanded. Shirley stayed active for more than 35 years and rose through the Chesapeake Bay Girl Scout Council.
where: Darryl organized “Bridging the Promise: Girl Scouts Then & Now” on Oct. 14, 2026, at Bethel United Methodist Church, where both the Black and white troops had once met.

topic: How many Black Lewes residents the records count
fact: During the height of the menhaden fishing industry, a 2023 Cape Gazette account estimated that more than 40 percent of Lewes was African American. Delaware Today, citing the 1960s census, put the share nearer 25 percent, and about 1 percent today. The two published estimates do not match. Both are far above the present figure. Fish-factory owner and mayor Otis Smith is remembered for jobs that could pay a mortgage, and for an open field the Black community used for baseball and picnics.
where: Darryl has presented the family photographs of that community. In 2023 he lent 70 of them to the Lewes Historical Society and said he hoped they would enrich the African American story of Lewes.

topic: The menhaden net reel
fact: A menhaden fish-net reel became a symbol of what Black workers contributed to Lewes. In 2022 a preservation board said the reel did not fit the rhythm of the Lewes Historical Society campus and voted to deny a request to keep it there. The mayor and council then let it stay, moved only a few feet.
where: Darryl compiled the episode into the Lewes Delaware Black History Timeline.

topic: A house bought by two people who had never been taught to read
fact: James “Alfred” Daisey and Lydia Coursey were never taught to read or write. In 1880 they bought a house in Lewes that the family still owns. Darryl’s genealogy follows the line back to Lydia’s grandfather, Mills Coursey, about 1773. Many family members were born in that house.
where: Darryl presented the Daisey Family History, including the family-tree slide, on Feb. 16, 2023.

topic: William S. Daisey and the Lewes bus line
fact: William S. Daisey, a brother of Darryl’s great-grandmother Sarah, served in World War I. The family believes he learned to drive in the Army. Mustard gas left him with complications that lasted the rest of his life and led to an early death. A 1920s photograph shows him beside the Hotel Rodney Lewes and Rehoboth Auto Bus Line, which he operated. After the war he bought a house in Lewes and married Elsie Stockley.
where: Darryl has shown that photograph in the family history he presents. The Cape Gazette published it from the Daisey collection in 2023.

topic: Chief William “Thunder Eagle” Daisey
fact: William Harrison “Bill” Daisey, Darryl’s father, was elected to the Nanticoke Tribal Council in 2004, chosen assistant chief in 2008, and became chief in June 2013. As Chief William “Thunder Eagle” Daisey he served until he stepped down for medical reasons in January 2016. He called it the biggest honor of his life. He was also, in 1987, the first Native American and the second person of color elected to Dover City Council.
where: The titles are in his obituary. Darryl presented the family history, including his father’s Nanticoke roots near Indian Mission Church, to the heritage commission in February 2023.

topic: Barney Ewell at the 1948 Olympics
fact: Henry “Barney” Ewell, who roomed at Lincoln Hall, won gold in the 4×100-meter relay and silver in the 100 and the 200 at the 1948 London Olympics. He was 30. Those three medals are still the most by a Penn State alumnus, and he also won four NCAA titles. The 1940 and 1944 Games, when he was in his prime, were canceled for World War II.
where: Darryl recorded the medals in African American Firsts and has spoken about Lincoln Hall, where Ewell lived, including at the 2017 NAACP lecture.

topic: Mary Godfrey, first full-time Black faculty member
fact: In 1956 Mary Godfrey was hired as an assistant professor of art education, the first full-time Black faculty member at Penn State. Seven years later, in 1963, English professor Charles T. Davis became the first Black faculty member to receive tenure.
where: Darryl compiled both firsts in Penn State African American Firsts in August 2010, a history he has presented in campus lectures.

topic: Eight students and Omega Psi Phi
fact: On March 15, 1921, Omega Psi Phi was established as the first Black organization at Penn State, and the campus’s first Black Greek chapter. It was reported that all eight Black students then on campus joined.
where: Darryl wrote this in Penn State African American Firsts.

topic: A cheer squad that said no, and the one that came later
fact: In April 1953, freshman Betty Love went to try out for the Penn State cheerleading squad and was told that “Negroes were not allowed on the squad.” The first Black cheerleaders — Paula L. Jones, Patricia R. Holloway, and Nelson Cox — were not selected until April 1971.
where: Darryl documented both moments in African American Firsts, the list he compiled in August 2010.

topic: The gold-colored can
fact: Elsie Daisey Draine lived to 101 and died in 2000. She left a gold-colored can of photographs that reached Darryl and his siblings in April 2022, the year after their father died. By February 2023 the family had posted more than 350 of the pictures. Trina Brown-Hicks, who helps run the Memories of Lewes page, said she had thought photographs from the 1920s, the 1930s, and even the 1800s were lost.
where: Darryl presented “A New View: The Daisey Family Legacy Photo Collection” at the Lewes History Museum on Feb. 13, 2025, and the family history in February 2023.

topic: Voices Heard, opening night
fact: Voices Heard opened at the Lewes History Museum on April 19, 2024, with about 30 photographs from the late 1800s to the 1960s, many shown in public for the first time and many on loan from the Daisey collection. Visitors were met by a late-1800s charcoal sketch of James “Alfred” Daisey and his grandson, William S. Daisey. Delaware Today counted 150 people, including members of Langston Hughes’s family. The historical society called the attendance a record for one of its exhibits.
where: Darryl, whose family is featured in the exhibit, said more than 100 people came and that it was “a positive portrayal of our history.”
